evidence: Varr. LL 5.172: ūnā dēmptā ūnciā deūnx (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Ac. 2.49: quom aliquid minūtātim et gradātim additur aut dēmitur
terms.comment: Varro explains the names of the fractions by it: eleven twelfths, deūnx, is the whole with one twelfth taken away. From a total, dē summā dēmere.

evidence: Liv. 6.15.10: dē capite dēdūcite, quod ūsūrīs pernumerātum est
terms.comment: The accountant’s word: deduct from the capital what has been paid in interest (Liv. 6.15.10).
Classically to draw off, take away; aliquid dē summā dētrahere (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s word for subtract.

evidence: Comen. OP 101: addendō, subtrahendō, multiplicandō, dīvidendō
terms.comment: Classically to draw away from under, to withdraw (Lewis & Short); Lewis & Short gives no classical instance of the arithmetic sense, but later arithmetic used it, and English takes subtract from it.

phrases.latin: sī dē quīncūnce remōta est ūncia, quid superat? … — triēns. — eu! rem poteris servāre tuam. redit ūncia, quid fit? — sēmis
phrases.english: If one twelfth is taken from five twelfths, what is left? — A third. — Well done! You’ll be able to look after your money. Put the twelfth back: what does it make? — A half.
